_comment: Guided tour for the Spot Finder. Steps point at real controls and wait for the user to press them — there is deliberately no 'do it for me' button, because someone who watched a button being pressed has not learned where it is. Read by chisurf.gui.widgets.tools.guided_tour.

steps.title: What this tool does, and what it does not
steps.text:
The Spot Finder answers one question: which pixels are an object. It finds molecules, beads or cells in an image and writes them — with their pixels — into the measurement's own file.

It fits nothing. The lifetimes come from Region MLE, the panel below this one, which fits the regions found here. Splitting them is the point: a detection you can look at, correct and re-use, and a fit that answers for exactly the regions it was given.

Eight steps, about two minutes. You press the buttons; the tour only points at them.

steps.title: Start with data whose answer you know
steps.text:
A segmentation is hard to judge the first time: regions appear over an image and there is nothing to compare them with.

So start with a simulated field — four objects at known places, with lifetimes of 1.0, 3.6, 2.2 and 0.6 ns, recorded on two detectors with the IRF measurement that belongs to them. It is a real photon stream written as an ordinary PTU, so nothing about the rest of the tour is a special case.

await.hint: Press 🧪 Load demo. The first time it simulates the scan, which takes a few seconds; afterwards the cached file is reused.

steps.title: The workflow is the recipe, not a pile of numbers
steps.text:
single_molecule is the standard one, and it is what the demo needs: smooth, threshold automatically, split objects that touch. It is the same pipeline the lifetime fit has always been run on, which is why a detection made here can be compared with older work.

Picking a workflow replaces every setting below with that recipe's. The fields are then your deviations from it — camera_spots measures each spot's own width for widefield data, objects does not split at all, which is right for cells.

steps.title: Look before you commit
steps.text: Preview detects in the first file only and writes nothing. It is how the settings get tuned: change a threshold, preview again, and watch the region count rather than guessing.

await.hint: Press 👁️ Preview, then open the Regions tab to see what was found.

steps.title: Four objects, outlined by what was measured
steps.text:
Each region is drawn as the ellipse with the same second moments as the object — its centroid, its axis lengths, its orientation. That is what makes the outline worth looking at: it shows what was measured, so a bad segmentation is visible rather than merely reported.

The list gives every region its area. Click one and the panel below shows its measurements.

steps.title: Click anything the detector missed
steps.text:
A threshold finds every object or none; you can see the one that matters. Click the image and a 2-D Gaussian is fitted to whatever is under the cursor — the click only seeds it, and the fit decides where the spot is and how wide it is, so a click two pixels off still lands on the object.

A fit that does not converge is refused with a reason. Nothing is placed where nothing was found.

await.hint: Optional: on the Regions tab, click a spot. Then press ➕ Add picks to make the picks part of the detection.

steps.title: Detect, and the regions are written down
steps.text:
Detect runs every selected file and writes each result into that measurement's own container — a label image and a table of measurements, joined by the region's label. Nothing is written beside the data as a loose file, and re-running the same settings replaces rather than accumulates.

Give the detection a name and two attempts on the same field can be compared instead of one overwriting the other.

steps.title: Every file gets a row, whatever happened to it
steps.text:
The Run tab has one row per input — ok, empty, failed or skipped — with the reason beside it. A file that found nothing says so; it never quietly leaves the list, because a batch that reports ninety of a hundred files looks exactly like a batch of ninety.

Now open Region MLE, below this panel: it fits the regions you just wrote, and the demo's lifetimes are 1.0, 3.6, 2.2 and 0.6 ns to compare against.
